items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.occasion: Keynote speaker introduction (FDIC Chairman Travis Hill), SMU 'Payments of the Future' symposium, Dallas Fed
items.quote: As the Federal Reserve System explores emerging technologies such as tokenization and smart contracts, we remain focused on balancing innovation with safety.
items.summary: Short welcome and speaker introduction at a digital-payments symposium the day after the January FOMC. Covers payments innovation and stablecoin regulation only; nothing on the economy or the rate path.
items.score_note: No monetary-policy content; official speech kept for coverage audit.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.occasion: Speech 'Outlook for the economy and monetary policy', FIA-SIFMA Asset Management Derivatives Forum, Austin (followed by moderated conversation)
items.quote: But right now, I am more worried about inflation remaining stubbornly high.
items.summary: Logan says she supported the January hold, that labor-market downside risks have meaningfully dissipated, and that policy may be very close to neutral and providing little restraint. If inflation falls and the labor market stays stable, no further rate cuts are needed; a cut could become appropriate only with material further labor cooling. On implementation she backs the end of runoff and reserve management purchases as technical, says purchases should not be mechanical and should track the TGCR-IORB spread, and calls for a centrally cleared standing repo option.
items.score_note: Pushes back on further cuts, sees policy near neutral and says inflation is the bigger worry, but is 'cautiously optimistic' the current stance works and does not raise hikes: +1, not +2.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.occasion: Moderated conversation, 10th Annual Bank Regulation Research Conference, Columbia University, New York (Reuters report)
items.quote: I'm not fully convinced that we're on a pathway to our 2% target
items.summary: Logan says policy is well positioned for the risks and she is cautiously optimistic inflation is on a path back toward target, but she is not fully convinced it will get to 2 percent because tariffs are still working through prices. She adds that the Supreme Court tariff ruling adds new uncertainty.
items.score_note: Hold is appropriate, but the only risk she stresses is inflation not returning to 2 percent; consistent with her Feb 10 'no further cuts needed' line. Mild +1.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.occasion: Speech 'The banking system and the demand for reserves', Eleventh District Banking Conference, Dallas (prepared remarks; companion essay with Sam Schulhofer-Wohl 'Options for reducing the size of the Fed's balance sheet')
items.quote: So, I favor an approach that reduces banks’ need for reserves and shifts the demand curve inward.
items.summary: Balance-sheet speech: the Fed holds $6.7 trillion in assets (21 percent of GDP) with about $3 trillion of reserves. Logan argues against returning to scarce reserves or reserve quotas and prefers shrinking the balance sheet by reducing banks' reserve demand, through more efficient liquidity rules and easier access to the discount window, intraday credit and standing repo; any change should be gradual. The prepared text says nothing on the rate path (she deferred that to the fireside chat that followed).
items.score_note: Prepared remarks are about balance-sheet size and reserve demand only; no rate-path content.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.occasion: Fireside chat with Robert Hulsey after her balance-sheet speech, Eleventh District Banking Conference, Dallas Fed (Reuters report)
items.quote: it's incredibly important to restore price stability, to get inflation back to 2% because stable inflation is just the bedrock for a strong economy.
items.summary: In the Q&A after her prepared remarks Logan says the Iran war raises risks on both sides of the mandate and that policy is positioned to adjust to the data as it comes in. She says she was not convinced inflation was heading all the way to 2 percent even before the conflict, and that US oil producers will not raise output much in the short run, so energy prices stay a near-term problem. A quick resolution would mean a moderate impact; a longer war would pull the two mandates in opposite directions.
items.score_note: Explicitly two-sided and wait-and-see ('positioned to adjust'); inflation is her chief concern but she gives no directional lean on rates here. Torn between 0 and +1, chose 0. Separate item from the prepared speech because the rate-relevant remarks came only in the Q&A.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.occasion: FOMC meeting April 28-29, 2026: dissent against the easing-bias language (8-4 vote to hold at 3.50-3.75%; Hammack, Kashkari and Logan against the guidance, Miran for a cut)
items.quote: who supported maintaining the target range for the federal funds rate but did not support inclusion of an easing bias in the statement at this time
items.summary: The FOMC statement records Logan (with Hammack and Kashkari) voting against the action: she supported holding the funds rate at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent but did not support keeping an easing bias in the statement. The quote is the Committee's wording of her position, not her own words; her own explanation followed on May 1.
items.score_note: Dissent against cut-leaning guidance while supporting the hold, not a dissent for a hike: +1. Quote is from the FOMC statement (Committee's description of the dissent).

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.occasion: Statement from Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan on FOMC dissent (April 28-29 meeting)
items.quote: In light of the two-sided risks to monetary policy, I believed the FOMC should not give forward guidance implying a bias toward rate cuts at this time.
items.summary: Logan explains she backed the hold but dissented from the 'additional adjustments' language because it implies the next move is most likely a cut. She is increasingly concerned about how long inflation will take to return to 2 percent: underlying measures were running meaningfully above 2 percent even before the energy and commodity price increases, and the Middle East conflict could add further pressure, while the labor market is stable. She says the next rate change could plausibly be either an increase or a cut.
items.score_note: Explicitly removes the cut bias and puts a hike on the table as equally plausible, but does not call for a hike: +1.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.occasion: Commencement address 'Look Up', Duke University Department of Economics, Durham
items.quote: Although the labor market is in balance, many employers are slow to hire. Inflation is still too high.
items.summary: Commencement address with career advice. The only economic passage notes a turbulent economy: a global energy shock from war in the Middle East, AI transforming jobs, a labor market in balance but with slow hiring, and inflation still too high. Nothing on the rate path.
items.score_note: Ceremonial speech; one descriptive line on inflation and jobs, no statement about the policy path. Kept for coverage audit.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.occasion: Opening remarks, 'Monetary policy and imbalances' panel, Bank of Japan IMES Conference, Tokyo
items.quote: Developing a richer toolkit in calm times would support a more nimble and targeted response to any future stresses.
items.summary: Logan says the Strait of Hormuz closure has cut global oil supply by nearly 13 million barrels a day and US producers can add little near term, so consumption may need to fall further. On Treasury markets she wants the FOMC to centrally clear its open market operations and to deepen tools that separate support for market functioning from monetary accommodation, flagging levered hedge-fund positions. She also discusses falling fertility and its effect on break-even job growth and the neutral rate. No statement on the near-term rate path.
items.score_note: No rate-path content; remarks concern energy supply, Treasury market resilience tools and demographics.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: CNBC 'Squawk Box' live interview (Reuters report)
items.quote: I do think there's a risk that the unemployment rate could pop from here
items.summary: Kashkari says inflation is still too high and its risk is persistence as tariff effects take years to work through, while the unemployment rate could 'pop' higher. He guesses policy is pretty close to neutral and says the Fed needs more data to see whether inflation or the labor market is the bigger force before moving in either direction.
items.score_note: Two-sided risks, policy near neutral, wants more data before moving 'whatever direction is necessary'. Time from the Minneapolis Fed schedule PDF.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: New York Times interview with Colby Smith (held Jan 13, published Jan 14; Reuters report of the interview)
items.quote: I don’t see any impetus to cut in January
items.summary: Kashkari says he did not want the December cut, sees no impetus to cut in January and calls it 'way too soon' for another cut, though one could be possible later in 2026 if unemployment jumps, especially if inflation also eases. He calls inflation staying above 2 percent for another two or three years very concerning, and says the Trump administration's threats against the Fed are really about monetary policy.
items.score_note: Pushes back on near-term cut talk and stresses inflation, while leaving a later cut possible: +1.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: Virtual town hall with the Wisconsin Bankers Association (Reuters report)
items.quote: we are really going to have to watch both sides of our dual mandate
items.summary: Kashkari expects pretty good growth and inflation heading down, though he does not know whether it reaches 2.5 percent by year-end. He gives no rate guidance, says both sides of the mandate need watching and that being too aggressive with rates could hurt the labor market. On the next chair: one vote, and the best argument wins.
items.score_note: Balanced, no lean on the rate path. Time converted from 11:00 a.m. CT on the Minneapolis Fed event page.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: CNN 'Erin Burnett OutFront' interview (recorded, aired 7 p.m. ET)
items.quote: And we need to continue doing our work to get inflation back down and hopefully keep the labor market strong at the same time.
items.summary: Mostly about Fed independence and Powell, whom he praises. On the economy he says inflation is still too high at close to 3 percent, a meaningful gap from 2 percent, and the job market is decent but cooling a little. No statement on the rate path.
items.score_note: Stresses the inflation gap but says nothing on rates and names both mandate sides; between 0 and +1, chose 0.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: Q&A with Jim Ryan, Midwest Economic Outlook Summit, Fargo-Moorhead-West Fargo Chamber, Fargo ND (MPR News report)
items.quote: Ultimately, we need to see where does inflation go?
items.summary: Kashkari says future rate decisions depend on whether inflation comes all the way back to 2 percent and whether unemployment keeps rising, levels off or falls. He calls Kevin Hassett's demand to discipline New York Fed researchers another step to compromise Fed independence and says the Fed will keep deciding on data and analysis. In a separate MPR interview that week he described cautious optimism and called Warsh a well qualified pick.
items.score_note: Purely data dependent, no lean. Time converted from 8:05 a.m. CT on the Minneapolis Fed event page.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: Bloomberg Invest conference, 'Monetary Policy First-Hand' conversation with Michael McKee, New York (Reuters report)
items.quote: I felt like policy was in a pretty good place and we have the luxury of just letting it gradually glide back to neutral
items.summary: Days after the US-Israel attack on Iran, Kashkari says he had a lot of confidence in the outlook until then: he came into 2026 expecting easing inflation to allow a single rate cut. Now the Fed needs to see how long and how big the new shock is, and whether it looks like Russia-Ukraine or like the Hamas attack. He warns that headline inflation staying elevated after five years of high inflation is a scenario to watch closely for expectations.
items.score_note: His prior of one cut (-1 flavour) is now suspended by the oil shock and an explicit inflation-expectations worry (+1 flavour); net wait-and-see. Time from the Minneapolis Fed event page.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: FOMC meeting April 28-29, 2026: dissent against the easing-bias language (8-4 vote to hold at 3.50-3.75%; Hammack, Kashkari and Logan against the guidance, Miran for a cut)
items.quote: who supported maintaining the target range for the federal funds rate but did not support inclusion of an easing bias in the statement at this time
items.summary: The FOMC statement records Kashkari (with Hammack and Logan) voting against the action: he supported holding the funds rate at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent but did not support keeping an easing bias in the statement. The quote is the Committee's wording of his position; his own essay followed on May 1.
items.score_note: Dissent against cut-leaning guidance while supporting the hold, not a dissent for a hike: +1. Quote is from the FOMC statement (Committee's description of the dissent).

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: Minneapolis Fed essay 'Why I Dissented' (April 28-29 FOMC)
items.quote: the FOMC should offer a policy outlook that signals that the next rate change could be either a cut or a hike, depending on how the economy evolves.
items.summary: Kashkari says he backed the hold but dissented because the 'additional adjustments' phrase is forward guidance pointing to a cut. Before the Iran conflict he saw policy as mildly restrictive and pencilled in one more cut in 2026 (December and March SEP). Now he sees two scenarios: a quick reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, where the right response is an extended hold and then gradual easing; or an extended closure, where rate increases, potentially a series, could be warranted to defend inflation expectations even at a cost to jobs. Signalling two-way risk could tighten financial conditions somewhat today.
items.score_note: Drops his own cut bias and says a series of hikes could be warranted in the adverse scenario, but his benign-scenario path is still hold then ease: +1, not +2.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: CBS 'Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan' interview
items.quote: I don't feel comfortable signaling that a rate cut is in the cards.
items.summary: Kashkari says everyone should be open-minded about where rates go: the longer the Strait of Hormuz is closed, the bigger the hit to US inflation, and in worse scenarios the Fed might have to go the other direction. The energy shock is by some measures already as big as after Russia invaded Ukraine; a CEO told him supply chains need six months to normalise even if the strait reopened today. The labor market is moving sideways at about 4.3 percent unemployment. He welcomes Warsh re-examining the dot plot and balance sheet, and calls the debt path unsustainable though not an immediate crisis.
items.score_note: Refuses to signal cuts and raises the possibility of hikes in worse scenarios, without calling for one. Time converted from the 9:40 a.m. CT slot in the Minneapolis Fed schedule PDF.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: Fireside chat Q&A, InvestUP CEO Summit, Northern Michigan University, Marquette MI (Bloomberg report)
items.quote: If the Strait of Hormuz is closed for an extended period of time, it may well be that the next move might need to be up in interest rates.
items.summary: Kashkari says that given the Iran war he does not know what the future holds for rates, and that an extended closure of the Strait of Hormuz may well mean the next move needs to be up.
items.score_note: Conditional openness to a hike, no call for one. Only the opening paragraphs of the Bloomberg story are open on this mirror.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: Minnesota Star Tribune interview with Emma Nelson (held May 8, published May 10)
items.quote: it gave me more concern that the language that had already existed in the statement was probably no longer appropriate, given the risk that I saw to the outlook
items.summary: Kashkari explains the path to his April dissent: in March he was comfortable leaving things alone, but by April the war was having a bigger impact on inflation and the global economy than he had hoped, and staff and Board analysis convinced him the easing-bias language was no longer appropriate. He says he is not shy about dissenting.
items.score_note: Restates the anti-easing-bias position on inflation-risk grounds; no new call for a hike.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: NPR 'Morning Edition' interview with Michel Martin, ahead of April CPI
items.quote: If the Strait of Hormuz is closed for an extended period of time, the next move may well be up.
items.summary: Kashkari says signalling that the next move is down makes financial conditions frothier than they should be, so the bias should come out of the guidance. Before the war he was fairly confident inflation was heading slowly to 2 percent; the war upended that. A cut would need the strait to reopen quickly or a real weakening in the labor market, which is holding at 4.3 percent unemployment. Fundamentals are otherwise good, with the data center buildout driving growth.
items.score_note: Wants the cut bias removed and says the next move may well be up if the strait stays closed; still conditional. Time is the page's publication timestamp.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: Q&A with B Kyle, St. Paul Area Chamber 'Lunch with Leaders', St. Paul MN (Reuters report)
items.quote: We are dead serious about getting inflation back down
items.summary: Kashkari says the labor market looks a bit better than earlier in the year while the Iran war has worsened inflation that was already too high. On whether Warsh will deliver the cuts Trump wants, he says the chair sets the agenda but is one of 12 votes and must persuade colleagues.
items.score_note: Inflation worse, jobs better, 'dead serious' on inflation: leans tighter, no explicit hike call. Time converted from 12:15 p.m. CT on the Minneapolis Fed event page.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: CNBC interview with Kaori Enjoji at the BOJ-IMES Conference, Tokyo (7:55 a.m. JST May 28)
items.quote: the labor market is in decent shape right now, while inflation is simply much too high
items.summary: Kashkari says he is focusing heavily on inflation, which has been above 2 percent for more than five years, while the labor market is in decent shape. The longer inflation stays high the greater the risk expectations unanchor, which would force an even more aggressive response, so the Fed is better off doing what it needs to now. Energy and fertilizer drive the current surge. On AI he is bullish long term but says it is too soon to know the policy implications. He would welcome a rethink of the dot plot.
items.score_note: Inflation clearly dominates and he talks of doing what is needed to keep expectations anchored; no explicit call to hike now, so +1 not +2. US Eastern date and time derived from the JST slot in the Minneapolis Fed schedule PDF; CNBC dates the article May 28.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: Korea University Distinguished Speaker Seminar, Seoul, moderated by Jinill Kim (Bloomberg report)
items.quote: I think it’s premature for me to conclude we need to be raising rates right away
items.summary: Kashkari says it is too early to conclude rates must rise and he wants to keep watching the data and the Middle East conflict before making adjustments, while keeping all options open. Reuters' version of the same remark adds that the situation makes him pay further attention to the risk that inflation keeps climbing and expectations become unanchored.
items.score_note: Pushes back on an immediate hike but the stated risk is all on the inflation side and hikes stay on the table. Torn between 0 and +1; kept +1 because the lean is tighter and only the timing is deferred. Time converted from 3:00 p.m. local in the Minneapolis Fed schedule PDF.

unverified.speaker: Neel Kashkari
unverified.what: Reuters interview with Leika Kihara in Tokyo (1:00 p.m. JST, i.e. just after midnight ET on May 27): 'Fed's Kashkari calls for focus on inflation risk, mum on timing of next rate move'. Search snippets say he called it far too soon to say when the next rate change comes while markets priced an October hike. Every open copy found (whbl.com, kfgo.com, marketscreener) returns HTTP 403 to curl, WebFetch and the browser pane, so no quote could be checked. Implied tone about +1.

unverified.speaker: Neel Kashkari
unverified.what: Wall Street Journal exclusive interview with Nick Timiraos (meeting on March 2 per his schedule): 'Kashkari Says Fed Can Sit Tight as War Clouds the Outlook'. Paywalled, no open copy found. Implied tone about 0.

unverified.speaker: Neel Kashkari
unverified.what: 'Office Hours' podcast interview with Chris Farrell (Heller-Hurwicz Economics Institute), recorded 2:00 p.m. CT; topics per schedule: Fed independence, current conditions, outlook. No transcript or report located.

unverified.speaker: Lorie Logan
unverified.what: Moderated conversation after her Austin speech (FIA-SIFMA forum). Bloomberg headline 'Fed's Logan Says Cooling Inflation Not Enough for More Rate Cuts'; Q&A remarks not checked separately, treated as the same occasion as the prepared text.

coverage_notes: Window 2026-01-01 to 2026-05-31. Dissent check from the three FOMC statements: January 28 (10-2, Miran and Waller for a cut) and March 18 (11-1, Miran) show Logan and Kashkari voting with the majority; April 29 was 8-4, with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan supporting the hold but opposing the easing bias, and Miran for a cut. The brief's context mentions only Logan's May 1 dissent statement; Kashkari also dissented and published 'Why I Dissented' on May 1. Each April dissent is entered twice by design, as in the A-series: the vote (April 29, 14:00, FOMC statement wording, not the speaker's own words) and the speaker's own explanation (May 1). Logan: all six items on the Dallas Fed speeches page dated January to May were opened, plus the releases page (one dissent release in the window). Her public calendar lists two further speaking occasions, both covered through Reuters reprints: February 20 (Columbia) and the April 2 fireside chat, which is entered separately from the prepared April 2 speech because the rate remarks came only in the Q&A. No Logan media interview was found; January (before February 10) and March have no policy remarks, and the Reuters tracker confirms no public comments from November 21 to early January. Q&A after the February 10 speech and the May 27 Tokyo panel discussion were not checked separately. Kashkari: Minneapolis Fed event pages are video only, so events are sourced from news reports; the monthly schedule PDFs for January to May were read in full and used for event times (time_et for his items comes from those PDFs or the event pages, not always from the quoted article). March after the 3rd and all of April have no public or media events on his schedule, and the Reuters tracker of April 21 confirms no comments since March 3. Not captured: January 4 ASSA panel on Bill Spriggs and January 9 fireside chat he moderated with the Xcel CEO (video only, no policy reports found); February 18-19 local interviews in Fargo (MPR, Fargo Forum, North Dakota Monitor, KVRR) and May 7 WZMQ; March 20 PBS Frontline interview (documentary); the May 2 MPR article only restates the essay. Two interviews are dated by publication, not by the day held (NYT January 14, Star Tribune May 10). The May 7 and May 29 items rest on the open first paragraphs of Bloomberg stories on the Bloomberg Law mirror. Kitco reprints carry zero-width characters; quotes were chosen to match after the pipeline's normalisation, and SRN copies were used where cleaner. investinglive.com was not used because its robots.txt disallows Anthropic agents. One web search was used; discovery otherwise ran on site listings, the Kitco off-the-wire sitemap and Google News RSS.
